# Apple Human Interface Guidelines

Use the relevant Apple guidance to make concrete design decisions. This package
contains a router, 13 family routes, 158 operational topic skills, and supporting
article-level references. It is
independent of Apple. The sources are a dated English HIG snapshot; check the
official source when a task depends on a newer release or a disputed detail.

## Route the task

1. Identify the target platform, device context, and user task from the request or
   project. Ask for the platform only when it materially affects the answer and
   cannot be inferred. Preserve the user's framework and product requirements.
2. Select the relevant family below and read that family's `SKILL.md`. Follow its
   link to the exact topic procedure under `.topics/` and read that `SKILL.md`.
   Apply its decision procedure, then consult its supporting article for facts
   and platform qualifications. Topic skills are explicitly read by installed
   file path; automatic nested discovery is not required.
   For platform support, product feasibility, or platform adaptation, first read each relevant
   platform's Getting started procedure, then the specific component or technology
   procedure. Check both the platform model and the surface's support limits.
3. Before finalizing the route, search the [complete topic index](references/topic-index.md)
   for the task's concepts as well as component or framework names. Its trigger
   descriptions connect everyday product requests to Apple's topic names; users
   need not name an Apple framework. Read the owning family and matching topic
   procedure before its supporting reference. Search relevant rows instead of
   loading the full corpus for a narrow question.
   For a screenshot-specific or animated example, also consult its
   [original visual explanation](references/media/index.md) when available.
4. Apply shared guidance and the target platform's documented differences. A
   missing platform subsection means no additional rule is stated; it does not
   prove support, nonapplicability, or identical behavior across platforms.
5. Compose families when the task crosses them: a component can also require
   accessibility, typography, localization, input, or system-experience guidance.
   Map the brief's material decisions to their owning topics. Read the owning
   procedure for each explicit concern, such as privacy or accessibility, as well
   as the affected components; a neighboring procedure's reminder is insufficient.
   Use [platform and task routes](references/platforms-and-tasks.md) when useful.
   In a review, map each supplied control to its candidate component procedure
   even when markup or behavior is missing. Use it to frame inspection questions;
   missing evidence neither proves a defect nor removes that control from scope.

All paths are relative to **this installed package**, not the shell's current
directory. No Python, network, sibling skill installation, or authoring cache is
required to read the guidance.

## Perform the requested work

Inspect the supplied brief, flow, code, specification or image before deciding
what is wrong or choosing a framework. Use the user's requested mode:

- **Design:** produce an implementable specification or interaction/state model
  from the topic's decision procedure, with concrete transitions and acceptance
  checks. Connect choices to the user's task and target platform.
- **Implement:** prefer the project's native system components when they supply
  the needed behavior. HIG explains experience requirements; verify API names,
  availability, and code against the appropriate SDK documentation. Make the
  authorized changes in the existing stack; a prose explanation alone does not
  complete an implementation request.
- **Review:** describe the observed problem, its effect, the relevant HIG rule,
  and a concrete correction. Separate source-backed findings from your own
  suggested improvements. Do not invent violations without inspecting evidence.
- **Adapt:** preserve the product task, data and useful state while applying the
  destination platform's interaction model. Patch the supplied artifact or give
  an explicit before/after contract when a design specification is requested.

Topic procedures are framework agnostic. Their worked examples and pseudocode
teach decisions, not a requirement to replace the project's technology. Load
related procedures only for a decision that actually depends on them.

Complete the topic's observable checks and report passed, failed and not executed
separately. Reading a file, citing Apple, or proposing a test does not establish
runtime behavior. Static code or screenshots cannot prove assistive-technology
order, native rendering, physical comfort, haptics, or SDK compilation.

Include official article/section links for material recommendations. Preserve
qualifications such as “consider,” “prefer,” and “avoid”; do not turn design
advice into invented universal requirements. Retain units and platform scope for
numerical specifications. If source passages conflict, describe the conflict
and the conservative application rather than silently changing the source.

## Source boundaries

This is comprehensive local guidance, not a verbatim Apple manual or an SDK API
reference. Original media explanations are supplementary to article references;
the source page remains useful for visual demonstrations. Source snapshots and
review status live in the repository's coverage report, outside ordinary skill
loading. Do not infer that a source has been independently reviewed just because
its local file exists.

Historical `navigation-bars` links now resolve to current Toolbars guidance;
`in-app-purchase` resolves to Apple In-App Purchase. The old Touch Bar and Messages
for Business HIG pages were unavailable at this snapshot. Do not fabricate their
current rules. Translations, archived pages, and complete linked SDK/WWDC libraries
are outside the source boundary.

# Make television choices visible from across the room

Read [Designing for tvOS](../../references/designing-for-tvos.md). Inspect the primary activity, content hierarchy, viewer/profile model, authentication, and input assumptions. Establish design, review, or adaptation mode and use supplied evidence to separate confirmed defects from untested remote behavior.

Rebuild the hierarchy around distant viewing and focus navigation. Prioritize legible titles and recognizable imagery rather than filling the TV with desktop density. Map directional movement and selection from each major region. The focused item must visibly identify both location and the available action through the platform's focus treatment; do not leave essential navigation dependent on pointer hover or tiny touch targets.

Choose the appropriate input contract. Siri Remote must support ordinary browsing; games may add controllers and relevant companion/voice input. Avoid making controller possession necessary for non-controller tasks. For long sessions or picture-in-picture, preserve the person's place when attention changes.

Reduce repetitive authentication using appropriate system integration. If the current system viewer changes, switch to the matching app profile deliberately and preserve privacy boundaries. Add Top Shelf, TV-app discovery, provider support, or SharePlay only when the content/activity warrants it, with a destination that matches the selected item.

**Before → decision → after:** A cooking-video app uses small tab labels, pointer hover menus, and one permanently signed-in household profile. Decision: across-room remote browsing and changing viewers require explicit focus routes and profile ownership. After, clear focusable categories lead into large recipe artwork, Select starts the highlighted recipe, and a viewer change updates saved recipes instead of exposing another person's history.

Deliver a focus-route map and corrected screen/profile flow or implementation. Fail if focus is invisible, a region has no remote exit, or a viewer change retains another profile's personal content. Check actual remote traversal, television legibility, and focus enlargement on supported hardware; a desktop screenshot only supports visual hypotheses.

For detailed movement use [Focus and selection](../../../apple-hig-inputs/.topics/apple-hig-focus-and-selection/SKILL.md) and [Remotes](../../../apple-hig-inputs/.topics/apple-hig-remotes/SKILL.md); for shared viewing use [SharePlay](../../../apple-hig-technologies/.topics/apple-hig-shareplay/SKILL.md).

name: apple-hig-focus-and-selection

# Keep the interaction target distinct from the chosen value

Read [Focus and selection](../../references/focus-and-selection.md). Inspect platform/input, focus groups, selected state, dynamic content, and supplied implementation. Establish design/review/adaptation mode. The guide's component-focus model excludes iOS/watchOS; visionOS gaze hover is a different system.

Map focus movement separately from activation and persistent selection. Focus may select automatically only when that does not unexpectedly shift context; tvOS normally needs separate activation. Use system effects and avoid moving focus without input. If an item disappears during discrete directional movement, choose a nearby one-step target; for other input, hide the indicator rather than inventing the next destination.

On iPad, group custom content so Tab moves among logical groups and arrows move within them in expected reading order; prioritize the likely entry item. Ordinary content focus coexists with Full Keyboard Access for all controls. On TV, every interactive item needs directional reachability and room for enlarged focus art. Keep unfocused, focused, pressed, selected, and unavailable states distinct. Full-screen gestures should manipulate visible content rather than invisible focus.

**Worked transformation:** Before, a TV watchlist opens each item as focus passes over it and uses the same glow for focus and Saved. Decision: navigation must not activate content, and persistent choice must survive focus movement. After, focus raises/highlights the item, Select opens it, and a filled saved indicator remains as focus moves; unavailable items are inactive and unreachable.

Deliver a focus-route/group map and state contract or implementation. Walk each entry, direction, activation, return, and removal scenario. Fail if a control cannot be reached/exited, focus jumps without input, selected state vanishes with focus, or enlargement obscures information. Source inspection can establish intended grouping; actual focus engines, remote behavior, and Full Keyboard Access need supported execution.

Use [Remotes](../apple-hig-remotes/SKILL.md) for TV button meanings, [Keyboards](../apple-hig-keyboards/SKILL.md) for shortcuts/access, or [Eyes](../apple-hig-eyes/SKILL.md) when the request actually concerns gaze feedback.

# Preserve deliberate remote actions across browsing and playback

Read [Remotes](../../references/remotes.md). Inspect the TV hierarchy, playback/game state, remote mappings, and requested design/review/adaptation. This is tvOS-specific. Preserve the existing stack and distinguish a remote press from accidental surface contact or movement.

Map swipes to predictable directional focus/scrolling with corresponding feedback; strength can govern scrolling momentum. Use presses for deliberate activation. Avoid acting on taps during live playback because passing or resting a remote can produce them. Press-then-swipe enters scrubbing; preserve the relationship between gesture and visible media position.

Define Back by hierarchy and task state. In ordinary browsing, Back opens the parent, not necessarily the last screen visited; root returns Home. During gameplay, Back may open a pause menu, Back from that menu resumes, and an additional deliberate action can leave for the game menu. Holding Back retains its system Home behavior. Play/Pause must control active media; game-specific secondary/skip use needs appropriate context.

If an electronic program guide exists, guide/browse buttons open it and page buttons navigate it. During playback, those page requests change channels. Without a guide, preserve system routing to the default guide app rather than inventing unrelated meanings.

**Before → decision → after:** A streaming app treats every clickpad tap as Pause and makes Back jump to a recently searched page rather than the show's parent. Decision: accidental touches should not interrupt viewing and hierarchy must remain predictable. After, deliberate Play/Pause controls playback, presses activate, and Back from the episode returns to its show; guide/page behavior follows the active context.

Deliver a state-by-button/gesture mapping and corrected interaction artifact. Walk browse, play, scrub, pause, and return routes. Fail if incidental contact changes playback, Back strands the person or exits unexpectedly, or a program-guide button performs an unrelated action. Actual Siri Remote gestures, momentum, and across-room feedback need hardware testing; keyboard simulation is partial evidence.

Use [Focus and selection](../apple-hig-focus-and-selection/SKILL.md) for directional reachability or [Game controls](../apple-hig-game-controls/SKILL.md) for controller/menu consistency.

# Preserve item identity through layout changes

Read [the collection guide](../../references/collections.md). The workflow is application advice, with documented support qualified by platform.

Inspect actual items, screen/code, target input/platform, and create/review/adapt intent. Determine whether visual recognition or text comparison drives selection; record selection, reorder, insertion, and scrolling behavior only when evidenced. Text-heavy comparison may belong in a list/table rather than a collection.

Choose a familiar row/grid before a custom arrangement. Size cells around meaningful imagery and labels, allowing focus/hover expansion without collision. Retain standard selection/editing interactions and use custom gestures only for a demonstrated task need. For iOS/iPadOS layout changes during manipulation, favor explicit triggers and preserve the person's location and selected item; do not reshuffle a live grid merely because a data property changed. The guide marks collections unsupported on watchOS, so adapt to a suitable list rather than assert parity.

Implement a requested collection or produce a cell/layout/interaction specification; review findings must name affected items or transitions. Specify stable identity and understandable insertion/deletion/reorder feedback as application decisions consistent with the guide.

**Worked transformation:** Before: a wallpaper grid reorders by popularity while someone drags an image, causing the target to move. Decision: dynamic ranking conflicts with manipulation. After: preserve the displayed order during the drag and expose an explicit refresh/sort action; animate a deliberate reorder while retaining selection.

Deliver the artifact and layout-change policy. Verify long labels, odd item counts, focused edge cells, reorder, and deletion of the selected item. Fail for overlapping focused cells, accidental activation during scrolling, or identity/location lost after a layout change. Report native focus/gesture execution separately from inspected logic.

Use [lists-and-tables](../apple-hig-lists-and-tables/SKILL.md) for text comparison, [image-views](../../../apple-hig-content/.topics/apple-hig-image-views/SKILL.md) for fitting, or [drag-and-drop](../../../apple-hig-patterns/.topics/apple-hig-drag-and-drop/SKILL.md) for transfer behavior.

# Design the whole focused unit

Read [the lockup guide](../../references/lockups.md). Lockups are tvOS-specific; the procedure below is application advice for that component, not a cross-platform support claim.

Inspect the supplied content, focus/navigation arrangement, platform, and create/review/adapt request. Identify the atomic unit people choose and its header/content/footer. Obtain both focused and unfocused states or mark expansion/tilt unknown.

Choose a card for combined review/rating content, caption button for titled content, monogram for a person, or poster for artwork-led choice. Keep dimensions consistent within a logical group while fitting the actual content. A monogram should prefer an available portrait with initials as fallback. A poster's optional title/subtitle can appear on focus; essential identity must remain understandable in context. Set caption-button focus tilt to the row, stack, or grid navigation direction and reserve enough space for the entire unit's expansion without neighboring overlap.

Implement the lockup, provide focused/unfocused annotated layouts, or report concrete expansion and identity defects. For adaptation to another platform, retain the content relationship using an appropriate supported component rather than calling it a native lockup.

**Worked transformation:** Before: a TV cast grid scales portraits alone while their names remain stationary and the focused portrait covers its neighbor. Decision: portrait and labels are one focusable person. After: group them as monograms that grow together, use consistent cell sizing, and reserve expansion space; missing portraits use initials.

Deliver the chosen form, focus bounds, content hierarchy, and activation outcome. Navigate every edge/corner and verify neighboring content, readable labels, and fallback identity. Fail for overlapping focus states, header/footer detached from content, or inaccessible unnamed choices. Linux layout inspection cannot prove remote-input tilt or native TV focus behavior.

# Operate on buttons

Read [the buttons guide](../../references/buttons.md) before making HIG claims. This procedure is application advice for turning that guide into an artifact; platform facts and dimensions come from the guide. Preserve the user's framework and authorized scope.

## Establish the action contract

Inspect the supplied screen, code, prototype, or brief. Identify the target platform, input methods, surrounding task, and requested mode: create, review, or adapt. For each consequential button, record its visible label or symbol, activation outcome, affected object, reversibility, current role/default status, and actual hit region if available. A screenshot can establish visible styling; it cannot establish hit geometry, keyboard behavior, or accessible names. Mark those as unknown and inspect implementation when available.

Classify the action before styling it. An immediate command fits a button. A persistent on/off setting may need a toggle; choosing one of several persistent options may need a segmented control or picker; a menu-opening control needs the corresponding menu button behavior. Retain a button when its action is to open that choice, but distinguish opening from committing a choice.

## Make and apply the consequential choices

1. Write an outcome-specific short verb phrase, or use a familiar symbol whose meaning survives its context. Give an icon-only control an accessible name that states the action. Do not assume a tooltip replaces the name. On Mac, an ellipsis indicates that another window, view, or app requires further input; add it based on the continuation, not merely because an operation takes time.
2. Assign semantic roles from consequences. Prefer one or two prominent likely actions per view and use style rather than unequal sizes to rank related choices. A primary/default action should normally be the likely nondestructive choice. If destruction is involved, consult the alerts topic before deciding confirmation and Return behavior: the guide explicitly allows a deliberate-destruction alert exception, so “destructive can never be default” is not a universal rule. Cancel abandons the current task; it is not a generic label for completing it.
3. Choose the system control/style when available, retaining its states and accessibility behavior. For a custom control, specify perceivable press feedback and preserve meaningful focus, enabled/disabled, and selected states as applicable. State the reason for a disabled action when the surrounding context does not explain it. This is application advice, not a new Apple requirement to add all states to every button.
4. Check visual and selectable geometry separately. Apply the guide's target and separation rules for the actual platform; a small glyph or small visual style does not establish a small hit region. On visionOS, retain a discernible shape/fill, use standard audible/state feedback, and inspect center spacing and hover overlap. Do not propose unsupported custom hover effects or haptics there. On watchOS, choose inline versus toolbar placement deliberately; preserve common heights for peer controls and use short labels for side-by-side actions. On Mac, distinguish view-body square/image/help buttons from toolbar items; apply the help-button placement/count rules only when designing Help.
5. Only when the command has delayed completion, define the initiating, waiting, and resolved behavior. On iOS/iPadOS, use the activating button's activity indication as described in the guide, preserving context and replacing its image when appropriate. Specify how duplicate activation is handled and what success or failure means in the product; do not promise network completion from a press animation.

Perform the authorized work: implement the controls in the supplied project for a build request; produce an annotated control specification for a design request; or report evidence-backed defects and exact corrections for a review. For adaptation, map each affected control to its destination platform rather than copying appearance alone.

## Deliver and verify

Return the changed artifact or a compact button contract containing label/name, outcome, role/default, style/placement, target region, and relevant state behavior. In review mode attach findings to identifiable controls and separate observed defects from checks requiring execution.

Verify that activation reaches the named outcome; cancellation leaves the intended prior state; keyboard/default activation cannot commit an unintended outcome; focus and accessible names identify the action; and enlarged labels do not clip or overlap adjacent targets. Measure hit regions from layout/runtime data when available. Fail the design if a destructive consequence is mislabeled, peer targets overlap, an icon has no discoverable name, or custom press feedback is absent. State separately which checks were inspected in source, exercised, or remain Apple-device checks; Linux inspection does not prove gaze, VoiceOver, haptics, or native rendering.

## Worked transformation

**Before:** A Mac photo organizer has equally prominent `Go`, `Remove`, and `Close` buttons. `Go` opens export settings; `Remove` deletes a selection with undo; `Close` finishes editing metadata.

**Decision:** The labels hide three different contracts. Export requires further input; routine reversible removal does not by itself justify a confirmation alert; finishing edits should name completion. The export task, rather than removal, is the likely action on this screen.

**After:** Specify `Export…` as the prominent action opening export settings, `Remove Photos` as a lower-emphasis command with a visible Undo path, and `Done` for finishing metadata edits. Inspect actual save semantics before changing `Close` to `Done`. Verify the Return mapping, undo restoration, and that each accessible name matches the resulting action. These product choices are an example application, not facts about the unseen implementation.

## Conditional handoffs

Load alerts for consequential confirmation/default decisions; toggles or segmented-controls for persistent selection; pop-up-buttons or pull-down-buttons for menu-opening behavior; toolbars when placement belongs to window chrome; and accessibility when naming, focus, contrast, or target access needs deeper work. Keep this button contract as the input to the next topic.

# Designing for tvOS Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/designing-for-tvos) · Retrieved 2026-10-25. Design for a large high-resolution screen often viewed from 8 feet or farther away, including by people moving around the room. Entertainment, games, fitness, education, and home utility experiences can hold attention for hours; picture in picture can coexist with another activity. ## Best practices - Make the entire interface legible and understandable across the room. Use rich edge-to-edge imagery, subtle fluid motion, and engaging audio for a cinematic result. - Work with Siri Remote gestures and the tvOS focus system. A clear focused item should highlight and enlarge as people navigate so location and available action stay apparent. - Accommodate game controllers, voice, and companion-device apps as appropriate inputs. - Make authentication infrequent and easy. Support shared sign-in and switch the app’s profile when the system’s current viewer changes. - Integrate TV-app discovery, SharePlay, Top Shelf, and TV-provider account support when relevant. ## Resources Consult the [official article](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/designing-for-tvos) for linked Apple design assets and implementation resources. #### Related The official article links the adjacent HIG topics relevant to this guidance. #### Developer documentation Use the framework references linked by Apple for current API availability and implementation details. #### Videos Apple’s linked design sessions provide demonstrations and additional implementation context; no video review is implied here. ## Change log Source revision dates: September 14, 2022.

# Focus and selection Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/focus-and-selection) · Retrieved 2026-10-25. This is original application guidance based on the source text. Independent media review is recorded separately in the coverage report. Focus visually identifies an interaction target for component-based navigation with keyboards, remotes, and controllers. Focus can select an item automatically, except where selection would shift context; tvOS normally requires separate activation. Rings/highlights on tablet/Mac and depth/parallax on TV reflect their platform focus models. ## Best practices Use system focus effects unless customization is essential. Do not move focus without input. If a focused item disappears during discrete directional navigation, move to a nearby one-step item; with other input, hide the indicator rather than guessing the next target. Follow platform reachability conventions: keyboard content focus on iPad/Mac coexists with Full Keyboard Access for all controls, whereas tvOS requires directional access to every interactive item. Use rings for text/search and usually full-row highlights for lists/collections. Standard focused/unfocused selection colors preserve active context. ## Platform considerations The source marks focus unsupported on iOS/watchOS in this topic’s sense. ### iPadOS Since iPadOS 15, Tab moves between focus groups and arrows move inside a group. Group custom views to produce expected reading order, normally leading-to-trailing then top-to-bottom; a vertical stack may need one focus-group container. Set priority so a likely primary item receives focus when a group is entered. Halo effects outline an item and can be refined for shape, clipping, or badge overlap. A content-configured cell’s highlighted accent appearance is separate from a focus effect. ### tvOS In full-screen content, gestures should act on the content rather than invisible focus. Use component focus for menus instead of a tiny free pointer; a gameplay-specific pointer must be conspicuous and integrated. Allow room and high-resolution art for enlarged focus states. Represent unfocused (receded), focused (raised/lit/moving), pressed (immediate feedback), selected (persistent choice such as filled favorite), and unavailable (inactive and unreachable) states distinctly. ### visionOS Connected keyboards/controllers use the same focus system family. Looking at content uses hover feedback instead; do not treat gaze hover as keyboard/controller focus. ## Resources Consult the [official article](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/focus-and-selection) for linked Apple design assets and implementation resources. #### Related The official article links the adjacent HIG topics relevant to this guidance. #### Developer documentation Use the framework references linked by Apple for current API availability and implementation details. #### Videos Apple’s linked design sessions provide demonstrations and additional implementation context; no video review is implied here. ## Change log Source revision dates: October 24, 2023, June 21, 2023.

# Remotes Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/remotes) · Retrieved 2026-10-25. This is original application guidance based on the source text. Independent media review is recorded separately in the coverage report. The Siri Remote combines physical buttons and a touch-sensitive clickpad for tvOS navigation, selection, and playback across the room. ## Best practices Preserve standard gestures and focus direction outside specialized gameplay. Provide clear feedback connecting gesture to content. Presses indicate deliberate activation; resting/moving/passing the remote can cause accidental taps, so avoid acting on taps during live playback. Positional up/down/left/right taps can help only when intuitive and discoverable. Back normally opens the hierarchy’s parent, which is not always the previously visited screen; at the root it returns Home. During play, Back can open a pause menu to avoid accidental exits; Back from that menu resumes, while another deliberate action can return to the game menu. Holding Back reaches Home. Play/Pause must play, pause, or resume active media. ## Gestures Swipe scrolls with momentum based on swipe strength; vertical swipes along an edge accelerate through many items. Press activates or selects, and pressing before swiping enters scrubbing. ## Buttons Touch-surface swipe navigates/changes focus in apps and acts like a D-pad in games. Surface press activates/deepens navigation or acts as the game primary button. Back handles parent/exit or pause/resume according to context. Play/Pause controls media, while games may use it as a secondary action or to skip an intro. ## Compatible remotes For an app with an electronic program guide, guide/browse buttons open it; page-up/down navigate within it, also supported by upper/lower surface taps. Without an EPG, the system sends those requests to the default guide app. While content is playing, page-up/down should change channels rather than page through the guide. ## Platform considerations This source is tvOS-specific and marks the other five platforms unsupported. ## Resources Consult the [official article](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/remotes) for linked Apple design assets and implementation resources. #### Related The official article links the adjacent HIG topics relevant to this guidance.

# Collections Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/collections) Snapshot: 2026-10-25. Original implementation guidance derived from the source. A collection presents ordered content in a flexible visual layout, particularly well suited to imagery. ## Best practices Prefer the familiar horizontal row or grid before inventing a layout. Text-heavy content usually scans more efficiently in a table or list. Make items easy to reach and choose, leaving enough space around images for focus and hover effects to remain visible without overlap. Preserve standard selection, editing, and scrolling interactions; add custom gestures only where the task needs them. Standard insertion, deletion, and reorder animations can explain changes, with custom animation available when appropriate. ## Platform considerations No additional macOS, tvOS, or visionOS rules are specified. Collections are unsupported in watchOS. ### iOS, iPadOS Treat dynamic layout changes cautiously. Keep changes understandable and easy to follow, and prefer an explicit user action as their trigger while someone is viewing or manipulating content. ## Resources Official implementation links and revision metadata follow. #### Related [Lists and tables](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/lists-and-tables) [Image views](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/image-views) [Layout](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/layout) #### Developer documentation — UIKit — AppKit

# Lockups Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/lockups) Snapshot: 2026-10-25. Original implementation guidance derived from the source. A tvOS lockup combines content, a header above it, and a footer below it into one focusable unit; all parts grow and shrink together as focus changes. Available forms include cards, caption buttons, monograms, and posters. ## Best practices Reserve enough spacing for the focused unit to expand without displacing or overlapping neighbors. Keep dimensions consistent within a row or logical group. ## Cards Use a card's combined header, content, and footer to present media ratings or reviews. ## Caption buttons A caption button presents image or text content with a title and optional subtitle below. Match focus tilt to the navigation arrangement: vertical movement for vertical stacks, horizontal movement for rows, and both axes for grids. ## Monograms Identify people with a circular portrait and name; use initials as a fallback when no portrait exists. Prefer a real image when available because it creates a stronger connection to the person. ## Posters A poster presents an image; optional title and subtitle appear upon focus. Size the poster for its actual content rather than assuming a universal aspect or dimension. ## Platform considerations Lockups are specific to tvOS and unsupported in iOS, iPadOS, macOS, visionOS, and watchOS. ## Resources Official implementation links and revision metadata follow. #### Related [Designing for tvOS](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/designing-for-tvos) [Layout](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/layout) #### Developer documentation — TVUIKit — TVUIKit

# Buttons Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/buttons) Snapshot: 2026-10-25. Original implementation guidance derived from the source. ## Contents - [Best practices](#Best-practices) - [Style](#Style) - [Content](#Content) - [Role](#Role) - [Platform considerations](#Platform-considerations) A button performs an immediate action. Its visual style, visible symbol/text, and semantic role work together to explain what activation does. ## Best practices Allow enough surrounding space for clear separation and easy selection. General hit regions should be at least 44×44 pt; visionOS targets need 60×60 pt. Custom buttons always need press feedback. ## Style Prefer system styles for built-in states, accessibility, and appearance adaptation. Use one or two prominent buttons per view for likely actions. Distinguish a preferred option through style rather than making related buttons different sizes. Keep label colors distinct from colorful content; the default monochrome often works best over rich backgrounds. ## Content Use a familiar symbol for a familiar action; use a short title-case verb phrase when words are clearer. Mac and visionOS can provide brief hover tooltips; text-labeled buttons usually explain themselves. ## Role Normal has no special meaning; primary is the expected/default action; Cancel abandons the current action; destructive signals data loss. Roles affect rendering, such as accent fill for primary and red for destructive. Primary can respond to Return and close a temporary view. Generally assign primary only to a nondestructive likely action. Application advice: consult the alert-specific deliberate-destruction exception before prescribing confirmation behavior. ## Platform considerations No additional tvOS rules are specified. ### iOS, iPadOS For delayed completion, show an activity indicator within the activating button, optionally changing its label to the current operation. The indicator replaces any button image while preserving context for the wait. ### macOS #### Push buttons The standard push button can show text, imagery, or both and can serve as default. Use flexible height for tall icons or multiple text lines, otherwise retain standard sizing. Append an ellipsis when the button opens another window/view/app for further input. Consider spring loading through a dragged selection plus force-click on Magic Trackpad, preserving the drag afterward. #### Square buttons These small glyph-only controls affect a nearby view, for example adding/removing table rows. They can act as push, toggle, or pop-up controls. Use them in the body rather than the frame, toolbar, or status bar. Prefer system symbols and omit introductory labels when proximity explains the function. #### Help buttons Use the familiar system question-mark control, at most one per window, opening context-specific help when possible and top-level help otherwise. In a dialog with dismissal controls, place it in the opposite lower corner, aligned vertically with those controls. Without dismissal controls, or in settings, use either lower corner. Keep it in the view body and omit explanatory introductory text. #### Image buttons Image buttons can act as push, toggle, or pop-up controls inside a view. Toolbar imagery instead belongs to a toolbar item. Allow about 10 pixels between image and clickable button edges and generally omit a visible system border. Put any needed label beneath the image. ### visionOS Buttons normally have a visible background and audible feedback. Circle suits glyph-only content, rounded rectangle or capsule suits text, and capsule suits text plus glyph. Standard states supply feedback; custom hover effects are not supported. A look-triggered tooltip can explain a glyph. | Shape | Supported visual sizes | | --- | --- | | Circle | Mini 28 pt; small 32 pt; regular 44 pt; large 52 pt; extra large 64 pt | | Text capsule | Small 32 pt; regular 44 pt; large 52 pt | | Text-and-icon capsule | Regular 44 pt; large 52 pt | | Rounded rectangle | Small 32 pt; regular 44 pt; large 52 pt | Visual size does not remove the 60-pt targeting requirement. Use a discernible shape/fill except inside a larger clearly bounded toolbar, menu, alert, or ornament. On window glass, thin material suits the button; floating in space, use glass. Reserve white fill with black content for the system's toggled state. Prefer round/capsule forms for steady gaze, and a capsule for a standalone button. Keep centers at least 60 pt apart; add 4 pt padding around buttons 60 pt or larger to prevent hover overlap. Avoid rows/stacks of mini/small buttons. Prefer rounded rectangles for vertical text stacks and capsules for horizontal rows. Standard sounds matter because visionOS provides no haptics. ### watchOS Inline buttons are capsules with a contrasting material. Put corner actions in a toolbar so the system relocates title/time and gives controls Liquid Glass. Full-width buttons suit primary actions. Side-by-side buttons should share height and use short labels or glyphs; vertical one- and two-line buttons should also maintain common heights. Toolbar actions can navigate related areas or operate on current content. ## Resources Official implementation links and revision metadata follow. #### Related [Pop-up buttons](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/pop-up-buttons) [Pull-down buttons](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/pull-down-buttons) [Toggles](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/toggles) [Segmented controls](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/segmented-controls) [Location button](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/privacy#Location-button) #### Developer documentation — SwiftUI — UIKit — AppKit ## Change log Revision dates recorded by Apple: December 16, 2025, June 9, 2025, February 2, 2024, December 5, 2023, June 21, 2023, June 5, 2023.
